title: Cache saturation nonuniform-access probe (wip)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note capturing an exploratory runbook and results summary for an unusual throughput drop we observed under mixed sequence-length workloads. The focus: how KV cache eviction + nonuniform memory access (NUMA/DRAM channel) + long-tail reuse interact to produce short-duration memory-bandwidth storms that throttle token throughput.

Motivation / hypothesis:
- We saw transient 30-60% throughput regressions on p4d-like boxes when a small fraction of requests had very long prefix reuse (large KV residency) while the majority were short, high-concurrency requests.
- Hypothesis: eviction churn of large-residency entries causes many page-level DRAM activations hitting the same memory channel, degrading effective bandwidth and increasing DRAM row-buffer misses. Conventional eviction metrics (hit-rate) miss the transient bandwidth side-effect.

Key questions:
- Are regressions driven by host NUMA imbalance, by interleaved eviction writebacks, or by streaming DRAM reads due to KV fetch patterns?
- Can changing eviction granularity (page vs. object) and eviction pacing reduce bandwidth spikes without increasing latency?
- Are there simple runtime knobs (per-model coalescing window, local eviction backoff) that preserve tail latency while reducing bandwidth storms?

Test setup (machines / baseline):
- Instance: 8x A100 equivalent (NUMA: 2 sockets, each with 4 boards, local memory channels per socket).
- Workload: 80% short-gen (seq_len 128, low-residency), 10% mid (seq_len 512), 10% long reuse (seq_len 2048 with large KV and high cache residency).
- Runtime baseline: production KV cache with LRU-like eviction + immediate reuse-promote on hit.
- Observables: tokens/s, P50/P95 generation latency, LLC misses, DRAM_ACTIVATE, DRAM_READ_BYTES, memory controller bandwidth util, per-socket CPU stalls, kv-evict-rate (objects/sec), kv-evict-bytes/sec.

Measurements / perf counters collected (representative runs):
- Baseline run (no throttles):
  tokens/s: 100k
  P95 latency: 480ms
  kv-evict-rate: 980 objs/s
  DRAM_READ_BYTES: 1.9 GB/s average but spikes to 12+ GB/s for 200-800ms windows
  Row-buffer misses %: 42% during spikes (baseline 12%)
  Per-socket bandwidth skew: socket0 ~11.6 GB/s peak, socket1 ~2.1 GB/s peak
  Observations: bandwidth concentrated on socket0 indicating NUMA hotness from large-residency objects mapped to pages on socket0.

- Experiment A: paced eviction (limit evict-bytes/sec to 1 GB/s):
  tokens/s: 92k
  P95 latency: 510ms (more variance for long requests)
  DRAM_READ_BYTES spikes reduced (peak 3.5 GB/s)
  kv-evict-rate dropped, but higher cache pressure led to ~5% increase in cache misses for mid requests
  Notes: pacing smooths bandwidth but increases misses. Tradeoff is workload dependent.

- Experiment B: NUMA-aware placement (pin high-residency KV pages across sockets round-robin):
  tokens/s: 98k
  P95 latency: 460ms
  Bandwidth peaks moderate (peak ~6.2 GB/s per socket)
  Row-buffer misses 18%
  Notes: distribution helps but requires page-level migration; migration overhead observed when items move during runtime (~50-150ms cost for large objects).

- Experiment C: eviction granularity change (evict smallest-objects-first, avoid evicting large contiguous pages mid-flight):
  tokens/s: 101k
  P95 latency: 455ms
  DRAM spikes less severe; observed more frequent small evictions but less dramatic DRAM activation bursts.
  Notes: suggests that eviction of large resident objects (that happen to be colocated in same channel) is a major contributor to spikes.

Profiling notes / traces:
- Combined perf + kernel slab metrics showed eviction activity correlating with increases in llc misses and context switch spikes as background eviction worker threads kicked in.
- Flamegraph: eviction background thread consumed ~25% CPU in spike windows; object scanning pattern indicated scanning contiguous address ranges leading to hot DRAM pages.
- ftrace of pagefaults: page reclamation for large objects causes synchronous reads (not async) due to current reclaim path; this amplifies bandwidth usage.

Short takeaways (current thinking):
1) Bandwidth storms are a real second-order failure mode even when aggregate hit-rate looks fine. They are triggered by co-located large object evictions that activate many DRAM rows on one socket.
2) NUMA/placement matters — packing large KV entries into a single NUMA node amplifies spikes. Round-robin placement or page-interleaving reduces peak.
3) Eviction pacing smooths bandwidth but increases eviction latency & misses; better combined strategies needed.
4) Eviction granularity policy (favor small-object eviction or prefer objects that map to less-busy channels) is promising.

Concrete proposals to prototype:
- Per-socket eviction queues + backpressure: throttle eviction if local memory controller bandwidth > X% (X ~ 60%) while allowing remote socket eviction to continue.
- Hot-object scatter: on insert, scatter large objects across sockets by mapping their pages to different NUMA nodes (requires page allocation control at insertion).
- Eviction coalescing window: hold small window (200ms) to batch-promote reused keys and avoid evicting objects that show bursty reuse patterns.
- Async prefetch + reclaim: shift fetches for evicted entries to async background with rate limit, to avoid synchronous reclamation spikes.

Open experiments (next steps):
- Controlled microbenchmark to isolate DRAM row-buffer miss vs. streaming reads: synthetic kernel that scans object address patterns we observed. Measure impact of page coloring / hugepage usage.
- Simulate higher concurrency (2x) and mixed model tenancy to see interactions with other workloads.
- Implement prototype "per-socket eviction throttle" in a branch and run 24h soak to look for throughput regressions and missed-promote patterns.

Notes-to-self / operational checklist:
- Re-run workload with perf mem events + PCM to validate memory controller counters.
- Add more detailed per-request trace IDs to correlate specific long requests with subsequent spikes.
- Check kernel config: page migration cost and CONFIG_NUMA_BALANCING settings may influence results.
- Postmortem idea: when an outage happens, capture lightweight perf counter dump and list of top-10 eviction candidates to reproduce faster.

Unresolved questions:
- Is the primary issue eviction-read amplification or writeback pressure (dirty pages) causing stalls? Current runs point to read-side, but writeback spikes occur in some traces.
- Can we safely rely on hugepages to reduce row-buffer misses or will that worsen co-location artifacts?

Appendix: useful commands / snippets used during profiling:
- perf record -a -g -- sleep 30 (capture system-wide stacks during spike)
- echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/zone_reclaim_mode (test effect of local reclamation)
- numactl --membind=0 ./kv_load_test (force placement)
- tools/collect-bandwidth.sh --sample-ms 200 > /tmp/bw.log

References / links: see linked_artifacts above; also internal doc: confluence:RINF-kv-bandwidth-notes (draft).

Status: rough notes and early experiment results. Looking for feedback on prototype designs and permission to land a small per-socket eviction throttle prototype behind a flag for further soak testing.
